## Upgrade 1: Frequency-Dependent Squeezing via a Filter Cavity
A **resonant filter cavity** inserted in the squeezed-vacuum injection path, before the dark port of the interferometer.
The squeezed beam reflects off (or transmits through) this cavity, which imparts a frequency-dependent phase rotation to the squeezing ellipse.
This is precisely the phase response of a detuned Fabry–Perot cavity near its pole frequency $\omega_\text{pole}$.

A single-pole filter cavity with half-bandwidth $\gamma_f$ and detuning $\Delta_f$ chosen such that $\omega_\text{pole} = \sqrt{\gamma_f^2 + \Delta_f^2} \approx 2\pi \times 55$ Hz will rotate the squeezing ellipse by ~90° between the low- and high-frequency limits, tracking the optimal angle.
The required filter cavity length $L_f$ is set by the need for sufficiently low bandwidth:

For $\gamma_f \sim 2\pi \times 55$ Hz and demanding low additional loss (cavity round-trip loss $\ll T_\text{coupler}$), the needed finesse is $\mathcal{F} \sim 10^4$–$10^5$, requiring $L_f \sim$ tens to hundreds of meters.
With $L_f = 300$ m and round-trip loss from two 5 ppm mirrors = 10 ppm:
$$\mathcal{F}_\text{max} = \frac{\pi}{T + L_\text{rt}} \sim \frac{\pi}{10\,\text{ppm} + T}$$

Choosing $T \approx 300$ ppm gives $\mathcal{F} \approx 10{,}000$ and $\gamma_f = \frac{c \times 300\times10^{-6}}{4 \times 300} \approx 2\pi \times 75$ Hz — close to the 55 Hz target; fine-tuning $T$ adjusts this.

**The fundamental problem with frequency-independent squeezing:**
Injecting squeezed vacuum into the output (dark) port of a Michelson interferometer reduces quantum noise only in one quadrature.
Frequency-independent squeezing therefore **cannot** achieve 3 dB improvement at all frequencies simultaneously.
**The filter cavity solution:**
A detuned Fabry-Perot filter cavity rotates the squeezed quadrature as a function of frequency.
Below its pole frequency $f_c$, reflection from the cavity rotates the squeeze angle by ~90°; above $f_c$, it passes through with minimal rotation.

### Filter cavity design
The filter cavity must have a **half-linewidth (pole frequency) matched to 55 Hz**:
For a cavity of length $L$ with input coupler transmission $T$.
$$T = \frac{4\pi L f_\text{pole}}{c} = \frac{4\pi \times 400 \times 55}{3\times10^8} = 9.2 \times 10^{-4} \approx \mathbf{920 \text{ ppm}}$$
This is well within the range of standard mirror coating capabilities (input coupler at ~1000 ppm is straightforward).
**Round-trip loss budget** (critical — excess loss degrades squeezing):
Each reflection off a high-reflectivity mirror: 5 ppm loss.
For a linear (two-mirror) cavity with $N$ round trips at 400 m, the two end mirrors each contribute 5 ppm per round trip:
$$\mathcal{L}_\text{RT} = 2 \times 5\text{ ppm} = 10 \text{ ppm/round trip}$$
The cavity **loss rate** relative to linewidth determines the squeezing degradation:
$$\epsilon_\text{filter} = \frac{\mathcal{L}_\text{RT} / T_\text{rt}}{2\pi f_\text{pole}} = \frac{\mathcal{L}_\text{RT} \cdot c / (2L)}{2\pi f_\text{pole}}$$
More transparently, the **loss-to-linewidth ratio**:
$$\frac{\mathcal{L}_\text{RT}}{T_\text{input}} = \frac{10\text{ ppm}}{920\text{ ppm}} \approx 1.1\%$$
The effective additional optical loss from the filter cavity reflection:
$$\eta_\text{filter} \approx 1 - \frac{\mathcal{L}_\text{RT}}{T_\text{input}} \approx 98.9\%$$
The filter cavity contributes only ~1.1% additional loss to the squeezed beam.
